result.text:
Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 built the same gearbox. On screen, a tie. On the print bed, one of them came out as a single fused brick.

Fable is the pricier model and works through every detail. Opus costs less and builds exactly what was asked, nothing more.

> SPEC - one gearbox described in a paragraph: housing, shafts, three meshing gears
> SOLID - each model outputs the parts as separate watertight bodies, ready to export
> SLICE - both files pushed through the same slicer profile with no manual fixes
> PRINT - the whole gearbox printed in place as one job, identical filament and heat
> TURN - the finished assembly driven by hand to see whether anything actually spins

On the monitor the two gearboxes looked interchangeable. Teeth meshed, shafts lined up, nothing intersected.

Opus 5.5 modelled every part exactly to size. Exact is the problem: printed plastic swells, and a zero gap becomes a weld.

Its gearbox came off the bed as one solid block. Every gear was there, perfectly shaped, and none of them could turn.

Fable 5.1 left roughly 0.3 mm of air around each moving face without being told to. Its gearbox spun on the first try.

It also chamfered the bottom edges and split the housing so the gears can be serviced later. Neither was in the brief.

One model built the drawing. The other built the object the drawing is supposed to become.

Opus is the cheaper pick for drafts and blockouts. Fable’s 2.5x premium pays for that 0.3 mm and everything around it.

A render forgives everything. A printer forgives nothing, and it never grades on a curve.

The two files, the slicer profile and the clearance each model picked are packed into the thread.

opus 5.5 is insane for motion design. 0 keyframes.

this 10-second video follows one white dot through an entire UI motion system

toggle → slider → notifications → reply → keyboard → back to toggle

here's the prompt to recreate it ↓

<inputs>
Ask me for: a target value for the slider, three short notification messages, a reply to type, one accent color and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM. If I skip anything, use 100, "Slider - Reached 100", "Gravity - Something is falling", "Messages - What now?", "retry" and electric blue.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 10-second 2D UI motion film in 16:9. Place everything on a near-black canvas with a faint dot grid. Use charcoal controls, sharp white text, one blue accent and a white ball that moves through the entire film. A real cursor makes the opening click feel physical; the ball guides each transition that follows. Keep the UI clean and the impacts precise, with only small spring overshoots. Move the camera through one continuous layout so every interaction fills the frame.

Banned: hard cuts, stock footage, glows, particle bursts, disconnected transitions, excessive bouncing and blurry text during camera moves.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 10 seconds, with something happening on every major beat.

Toggle: the cursor clicks a blue switch. Its white ball springs free, and the camera follows it toward a horizontal slider.

Slider: the ball lands on the knob and moves it along the track. The blue fill stays attached, while a value bubble above the knob climbs to 100.

Notifications: hitting 100 sends the ball onward and brings in three dark cards: "Slider", "Gravity" and "Messages". Each arrives on its own beat. The camera follows the ball down to "What now?".

Reply: the small "Reply" pill stretches into a text field. A keyboard rises below it as part of the same scene.

Keyboard: the ball strikes the keys while "retry" appears in the field. It lands on Return, the blue send button activates and the reply contracts into a small blue message.

Return: the camera pulls back to show the toggle, slider, cards and keyboard together in one world. The ball travels back to the first switch. Match its position, the cursor and the switch state to the opening frame so the film loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. Make one HTML file at 1920x1080 and 60fps. Calculate every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Arrange all UI components in one world. Use a single camera transform with position and log-space zoom, making each close-up a move through that world.
3. Give the white ball one continuous route between the toggle, slider, cards and keys. Use closed-form springs for landings and a brief squash on impact.
4. Calculate the slider fill and number from the ball's horizontal position. Keep the tooltip centered over the knob until it reaches 100.
5. Give every key press a fixed time. Show the reply as the portion typed by that moment, so any frame can be rendered independently.
6. Align the click, slider movement, card arrivals, key taps, send and return with measured beats. Add a subtle UI sound to each contact.
7. Render one still per beat to check pacing and readability, then export the full film with Playwright at 60fps. Inspect fast camera moves and the loop boundary frame by frame.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never let the ball teleport between components: show the path of every handoff. Keep the value bubble attached to the slider knob. Leave enough space for the notifications to stay readable during camera moves. The keys the ball presses must match the text appearing in the field. Match the first and last frames, including the ball's direction and cursor position, to prevent a loop stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and four stills (toggle, slider, notifications, keyboard) before building the full video.
</start>

result.text:
6 parallelism strategies for LLM inference in production:

(popular LLM interview question)

Running a model across four GPUs does not merge their memory into one shared pool.

Each GPU has its own memory, so data stored on another GPU must cross the interconnect before a layer can use it.

This is the central trade-off behind parallelism. It removes local memory or compute limits but adds communication overhead.

The visual below explains the six common strategies for parallelizing LLM inference:

- Data parallelism runs complete model replicas on separate GPU groups. It increases throughput, but cannot make an oversized model fit.

- Tensor parallelism splits matrix operations inside each transformer layer. It reduces weight memory per GPU, but the GPUs must combine partial results throughout the layer stack.

- Pipeline parallelism assigns layer groups to different GPUs. Activations move between stages, while insufficient micro-batching leaves some stages idle.

- Context parallelism splits sequence positions in two ways. Prefill context parallelism divides a long input across GPUs to target lower TTFT. Decode context parallelism divides the stored KV history to increase cache capacity, but every decoder layer must merge partial attention results.

- Expert parallelism distributes MoE experts across GPUs. Token routing and uneven expert load add network cost and idle time.

- Hybrid parallelism combines multiple strategies in one deployment. For example, tensor parallelism can operate within a node, pipeline parallelism across nodes, and data parallelism across model replicas. This matches each communication pattern to the available links, but adds more coordination paths.

Production deployments often combine methods, but each one should fix a measured bottleneck.

- If the weights do not fit, use tensor or pipeline parallelism.
- If long-prompt prefill or KV-cache capacity is the limit, use the corresponding form of context parallelism.
- MoE models may need expert parallelism to place expert weights.
- If one replica meets its latency target but requests still queue, add data-parallel replicas.

Keep tensor parallelism on the fastest links. After each change, measure memory, TTFT, TPOT, and other metrics again.

Add another method only when measurements reveal another bottleneck.

I wrote a detailed article explaining how each strategy works, where communication occurs, and how to choose a layout for a real deployment.

Read it below.
